modules.title: Foundations & Core Mental Models
modules.why_here: These four concepts form the shared mental model every agentic AI interview assumes. They define what an agent is, why LLMs can drive one, how to distinguish agentic from non-agentic systems, and the foundational reasoning technique (CoT) that all patterns build on.
modules.capability: Explain what an agent is (autonomy, goal-directedness, environment interaction), why LLMs serve as reasoning engines and their limitations, distinguish agentic systems from chains/RAG/single-turn prompting, and describe chain-of-thought reasoning and its role in agentic behavior — using the precise terminology interviewers expect.

modules.title: Core Agentic Patterns
modules.why_here: These eight patterns constitute the complete single-agent repertoire. Each extends the foundation with a distinct capability (acting, planning, searching, correcting, remembering, retrieving knowledge, involving humans). Interviews test them comparatively — when to use which, how they compose, and their failure modes.
modules.capability: Compare and contrast the major single-agent patterns (ReAct, tool use, planning, ToT/GoT, reflection, memory, RAG-for-agents, human-in-the-loop), explain the prompt structure and control flow of each, describe when each pattern applies and how they compose (e.g., ReAct with memory, planning with reflection), and identify the characteristic failure modes interviewers probe.

modules.title: Agent Architectures
covers: Multi-Agent Collaboration Patterns (Debate, Hierarchy, Swarm, Sequential)
modules.why_here: Architectures compose patterns into runnable systems. Single-agent architecture is the baseline; multi-agent systems and their collaboration patterns (debate, hierarchy, swarm, sequential) are the other major interview axis. These three concepts are always discussed together — coordination, communication, and topology.
modules.capability: Diagram and explain a single-agent architecture (loop, memory, tools, planner, executor, state), describe why and when to introduce multiple agents, compare the four collaboration patterns (debate, hierarchy, swarm, sequential) on latency, cost, quality, and complexity, and justify an architectural choice for a given problem scenario.

modules.title: Frameworks & Implementation
modules.why_here: Frameworks map patterns and architectures to production code. LangGraph (graph-centric), AutoGen (conversation-centric), CrewAI (role-centric), and Semantic Kernel (planner/plugin-centric) represent four distinct programming models. Legacy LangChain and AutoGPT/BabyAGI provide the historical contrast interviews expect.
modules.capability: Compare the major agentic frameworks (LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, Semantic Kernel) on programming model (state graph vs. conversation vs. role-based vs. planner/plugin), explain why LangGraph replaced AgentExecutor, describe what AutoGPT/BabyAGI demonstrated and why they failed in production, and articulate the criteria for choosing a framework in a given context.

modules.title: Evaluation, Reliability & Emerging Standards
covers: Agent Benchmarks (AgentBench, WebShop, ALFWorld, τ-bench, GAIA, SWE-bench)

modules.why_here: This module covers the 'how do you know it works' and 'how do you run it in production' questions that distinguish senior candidates. Evaluation methodologies and benchmarks measure quality; failure modes, guardrails, and observability ensure reliability; MCP, A2A, and function calling standards enable interoperability. They share a concern: moving from prototype to production.
modules.capability: Describe agent evaluation methodologies (offline vs. online, LLM-as-judge, trajectory evaluation), identify which benchmark tests which capability (web navigation, coding, reasoning, tool use), enumerate common failure modes with their detection and mitigation strategies, explain guardrail patterns (input/output validation, tool confirmation, sandboxing), summarize MCP (servers, resources, tools, prompts), A2A (discovery, negotiation, transport), and function calling standard differences, and describe observability primitives (traces, spans, token accounting, replay debugging).

traversal.why: Foundations establish the mental model every interview assumes. Patterns build the single-agent repertoire interviews probe. Architectures compose patterns into systems. Frameworks map patterns to production tooling. Evaluation and standards cover the reliability and interoperability questions senior interviews increasingly ask.

modules.title: Foundations & Core Mental Models
modules.why_here: These four concepts form the shared mental model every agentic AI interview assumes. They define what an agent is, why LLMs can drive one, how to distinguish agentic from non-agentic systems, and the foundational reasoning technique (CoT) that all patterns build on.
modules.capability: Explain what an agent is (autonomy, goal-directedness, environment interaction), why LLMs serve as reasoning engines and their limitations, distinguish agentic systems from chains/RAG/single-turn prompting, and describe chain-of-thought reasoning and its role in agentic behavior — using the precise terminology interviewers expect.

modules.title: Core Agentic Patterns
modules.why_here: These eight patterns constitute the complete single-agent repertoire. Each extends the foundation with a distinct capability (acting, planning, searching, correcting, remembering, retrieving knowledge, involving humans). Interviews test them comparatively — when to use which, how they compose, and their failure modes.
modules.capability: Compare and contrast the major single-agent patterns (ReAct, tool use, planning, ToT/GoT, reflection, memory, RAG-for-agents, human-in-the-loop), explain the prompt structure and control flow of each, describe when each pattern applies and how they compose (e.g., ReAct with memory, planning with reflection), and identify the characteristic failure modes interviewers probe.

modules.title: Agent Architectures
covers: Multi-Agent Collaboration Patterns (Debate, Hierarchy, Swarm, Sequential)
modules.why_here: Architectures compose patterns into runnable systems. Single-agent architecture is the baseline; multi-agent systems and their collaboration patterns (debate, hierarchy, swarm, sequential) are the other major interview axis. These three concepts are always discussed together — coordination, communication, and topology.
modules.capability: Diagram and explain a single-agent architecture (loop, memory, tools, planner, executor, state), describe why and when to introduce multiple agents, compare the four collaboration patterns (debate, hierarchy, swarm, sequential) on latency, cost, quality, and complexity, and justify an architectural choice for a given problem scenario.

modules.title: Frameworks & Implementation
modules.why_here: Frameworks map patterns and architectures to production code. LangGraph (graph-centric), AutoGen (conversation-centric), CrewAI (role-centric), and Semantic Kernel (planner/plugin-centric) represent four distinct programming models. Legacy LangChain and AutoGPT/BabyAGI provide the historical contrast interviews expect.
modules.capability: Compare the major agentic frameworks (LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, Semantic Kernel) on programming model (state graph vs. conversation vs. role-based vs. planner/plugin), explain why LangGraph replaced AgentExecutor, describe what AutoGPT/BabyAGI demonstrated and why they failed in production, and articulate the criteria for choosing a framework in a given context.

modules.title: Evaluation, Reliability & Emerging Standards
covers: Agent Benchmarks (AgentBench, WebShop, ALFWorld, τ-bench, GAIA, SWE-bench)
Failure Modes (Hallucination, Tool Errors, Planning Failures, Loops, Cost/Latency)
modules.why_here: This module covers the 'how do you know it works' and 'how do you run it in production' questions that distinguish senior candidates. Evaluation methodologies and benchmarks measure quality; failure modes, guardrails, and observability ensure reliability; MCP, A2A, and function calling standards enable interoperability. They share a concern: moving from prototype to production.
modules.capability: Describe agent evaluation methodologies (offline vs. online, LLM-as-judge, trajectory evaluation), identify which benchmark tests which capability (web navigation, coding, reasoning, tool use), enumerate common failure modes with their detection and mitigation strategies, explain guardrail patterns (input/output validation, tool confirmation, sandboxing), summarize MCP (servers, resources, tools, prompts), A2A (discovery, negotiation, transport), and function calling standard differences, and describe observability primitives (traces, spans, token accounting, replay debugging).
